entries.title: Name the evidence
entries.why: An unnamed authority leaves the reader unable to check the claim.
entries.fix: Name the actual source and its limits, ask for it, or remove the unsupported attribution.
entries.keep_when: Keep when a named study or expert follows immediately.

examples.before: Studies show this may help.
examples.after: This may help; ask the author for the study before publication.

entries.title: Explain the relationship
entries.why: A repeated contrast can obscure what changed.
entries.fix: State the relationship directly while retaining the original distinction.
entries.keep_when: Keep a contrast that corrects a likely misunderstanding.

examples.before: It is not just a cost, but a risk.
examples.after: It is both a cost and a risk.

entries.title: Lead with the point
entries.why: Repeated announcements delay the useful information.
entries.fix: Remove the announcement if the following claim stands alone.
entries.keep_when: Keep a warning that signals a meaningful change in scope.

examples.before: It is worth noting that approval may take a week.

entries.title: Explain the consequence
entries.why: Generic significance does not explain the effect on the reader.
entries.fix: Use a supplied consequence, or cut the unsupported praise.
entries.keep_when: Keep significance supported by specific evidence in context.

examples.before: This marks a paradigm shift: approval may take a week.

entries.title: Read for rhythm
entries.why: Similar sentence lengths may make distinctions hard to hear.
entries.fix: Read aloud and combine or split only where meaning becomes clearer.
entries.keep_when: Keep parallel sentences in instructions, dialogue or deliberate repetition.

examples.before: The queue is full. The job may wait.
examples.after: The queue is full, so the job may wait.

entries.title: Check dash connections
entries.why: Many interruptions can obscure a sentence’s main connection.
entries.fix: Consider a period, comma or parentheses where the connection becomes clearer.
entries.keep_when: Keep a list separator, quoted dash or deliberate interruption when it aids reading.

examples.before: The queue is full — the job may wait.
examples.after: The queue is full; the job may wait.

entries.title: Choose a precise word
entries.why: A familiar general word may hide the action or property intended.
entries.fix: Use the precise term or an ordinary verb if it preserves meaning.
entries.keep_when: Keep technical terms such as robust statistics, quoted language and the author’s intentional voice.

examples.before: We must utilize the existing queue.
examples.after: We must use the existing queue.

entries.title: Rule of three
entries.why: General qualities can leave the reader without a concrete property.
entries.fix: Use actual supported properties, or keep a parallel list if it communicates them.
entries.keep_when: Keep factual triples, intentional rhetoric and technical categories.

examples.before: The service is simple, powerful, and flexible.
examples.after: Ask which specific properties the author means before replacing this description.

entries.title: Coordinated series
entries.why: A long sequence of actions can hide their relationship or cumulative effect.
entries.fix: Check the relationship between the actions; split only if that clarifies it.
entries.keep_when: Keep an accurate sequence of real actions or a deliberate cumulative rhythm.

examples.before: After testing, measuring, and reviewing, we may proceed.
examples.after: We may proceed after testing, measuring, and reviewing.

entries.title: Copula avoidance
entries.why: An indirect linking phrase may add words without clarifying a role.
entries.fix: Consider is when the original linking phrase adds no meaning.
entries.keep_when: Keep acts as or serves as when describing a temporary or functional role.

examples.before: The library serves as a hub.

entries.title: Cheerful opener
entries.why: An automatic acknowledgement may delay the requested answer.
entries.fix: Lead with useful information when an acknowledgement adds nothing.
entries.keep_when: Keep an acknowledgement that fits the relationship or dialogue.

examples.before: Certainly! Approval may take a week.

entries.title: Short fragment
entries.why: A short unit may be a complete sentence, dialogue or emphasis; length alone cannot decide.
entries.fix: Treat this as an annotation. Read surrounding units before changing it.
entries.keep_when: Keep complete short sentences, dialogue and a single punchy fragment.

examples.before: Still short.

entries.title: Summary close
entries.why: A generic closing announcement may repeat rather than complete the argument.
entries.fix: End at the useful conclusion if the announcement is unnecessary.
entries.keep_when: Keep summaries in reports and teaching material where readers need a recap.

examples.before: In conclusion, approval may take a week.

entries.title: Challenges future formula
entries.why: A generic transition can conceal what the next section actually covers.
entries.fix: Use the specific next point if the supplied material supports it.
entries.keep_when: Keep literal discussion of future challenges or venue-required headings.

examples.before: Looking ahead: approval may take a week.

entries.title: Repeated opening
entries.why: Repeated sentence openings can obscure changing relationships.
entries.fix: Check whether repetition supports emphasis before varying it.
entries.keep_when: Keep deliberate repetition, dialogue, procedures and learner exercises.

examples.before: We can read. We can vote. We can wait.
examples.after: We can read. We can vote. We can wait.

entries.title: Fragment pattern
entries.why: Several very short units may interrupt the argument.
entries.fix: Check which units are complete sentences and which fragments need connection.
entries.keep_when: Keep dialogue, slogans, instructions and deliberate emphasis.

examples.before: Still short. Not enough.

entries.title: Uniform paragraphs
entries.why: Similar paragraph sizes may hide differences in the argument.
entries.fix: Let each paragraph develop its point; vary only when useful.
entries.keep_when: Keep parallel reference entries, forms and technical explanations.

examples.before: The queue is full. The job may wait.
examples.after: The queue is full, so the job may wait.

entries.title: Bold inline headers
entries.why: Repeated bold labels may make navigation harder than real headings.
entries.fix: Consider semantic headings where readers need navigation.
entries.keep_when: Keep compact labels in forms, reference lists and venue-required layouts.

examples.before: **Status:** Approval may take a week.
examples.after:
## Status

Approval may take a week.

entries.title: Title case headings
entries.why: Heading capitalization may distract if it conflicts with the venue style.
entries.fix: Use the required or established heading style consistently.
entries.keep_when: Keep title case when the publication or naming convention requires it.

examples.before: ## Review The Queue Status

entries.title: List heavy
entries.why: Many full-sentence list items may hide how the claims connect.
entries.fix: Use prose when relationships matter more than parallel scanning.
entries.keep_when: Keep procedures, factual lists and accessible reference material.

examples.before:
- The queue is full.
- The job may wait.
examples.after: The queue is full, so the job may wait.

entries.title: Heading depth skipped
entries.why: Consecutive headings that jump more than one level confuse readers who rely on heading hierarchy for navigation.
entries.fix: Use one intermediate heading level, or restructure so the depth increase is justified by the content.
entries.keep_when: A deeply nested sub-section is the clearest structure even though it skips a level.

examples.before:
## Intro
### Details
#### Sub-Detail

entries.title: Inconsistent list markers
entries.why: Mixed list markers distract from the content and may mislead readers about list structure.
entries.fix: Use one marker style throughout: all hyphens, all asterisks, or all numbers for ordered steps.
entries.keep_when: A multi-level list intentionally mixes markers to distinguish nesting levels.

examples.before:
- item one
* item two

entries.title: Adjacent articles
entries.why: Repeated articles like 'the the' are likely typos that break fluency.
entries.fix: Remove the duplicate article, or check that a different word was intended between them.
entries.keep_when: A compound noun phrase genuinely requires two articles (rare).

examples.before: the the budget
a a report

entries.title: Wrong article before noun
entries.why: 'An' before a consonant sound like 'an policy' breaks reader expectations.
entries.fix: Use 'a' before consonant sounds and 'an' before vowel sounds, regardless of spelling.
entries.keep_when: The word after the article is an abbreviation pronounced with the opposite sound, e.g., 'a URL'.

examples.before: an policy
a hour

entries.title: Regional spelling variant
entries.why: Mixing American and British spellings in the same document can appear inconsistent.
entries.fix: Use the spelling that matches the declared dialect consistently throughout.
entries.keep_when: A direct quotation or proper name preserves its original spelling.

examples.before: colour
organise

entries.title: Common typo
entries.why: A word that matches a known typographical error pattern is likely misspelled.
entries.fix: Replace with the standard spelling.
entries.keep_when: The word is a deliberate variant: dialect, brand name, or quoted speech.

examples.before: teh
recieved

entries.title: Long clause chain
entries.why: Consecutive dependent clauses create run-on constructions that are hard to parse.
entries.fix: Break into shorter sentences or restructure to reduce nesting.
entries.keep_when: The chain is a deliberate stylistic choice for rhetorical effect, and the meaning remains clear.

examples.before: Because the report that was submitted by the committee that was tasked with reviewing the policy that was enacted last year...
examples.after: The committee submitted its report on last year's policy. The report...

entries.title: Dense passage
entries.why: A paragraph with many long sentences and abstract nouns is harder to read.
entries.fix: Add shorter sentences, replace abstract nouns with concrete verbs, or break the paragraph at logical points.
entries.keep_when: The density serves the subject matter, e.g., a statutory definition that must preserve exact wording.

examples.before: The proposed framework for the implementation of the new policy guidelines represents a significant step forward in improving the efficiency of the overall operational workflow across all departments.
examples.after: The new policy framework should improve workflow efficiency across all departments.
